title: Chapter XL

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth tells Jane of Darcy's proposal and of Wickham's true character. Jane is distressed for both men. The sisters agree not to expose Wickham publicly, since he is leaving soon. Elizabeth keeps back Darcy's part in separating Jane and Bingley.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter XL,” how does Austen show keeping secrets? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XL, how does Austen develop the idea of keeping secrets? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XL develops the idea of keeping secrets. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XL (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of keeping secrets. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XL suggests about keeping secrets. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and foreshadowing), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XL to complicate the reader's understanding of keeping secrets. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XL within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of keeping secrets responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XL alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of keeping secrets follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XL and its treatment of keeping secrets. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and foreshadowing, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XL as evidence for a larger claim about keeping secrets in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XL as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of keeping secrets. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: letters
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Letters carry news, reveal character and change minds; Darcy's letter is the turning point of the novel. In this chapter: “She then spoke of the letter, repeating the whole of its contents as far as they concerned” (Chapter XL, paragraph 9).

symbolsAndMotifs.name: marriage and money
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Incomes, entails and fortunes are stated precisely; marriage is always also an economic question. In this chapter: “Yes, yes. They will take care not to outrun their income. They will never be distressed for money. Well, much good may” (Chapter XL, paragraph 33).

followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Elizabeth now distinguishes between appearance and goodness. Useful evidence: “Elizabeth’s impatience to acquaint Jane with what had happened could no longer be overcome” (Chapter XL, paragraph 1): Opening. Theme link: the sisters debate what to do with what they know. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

items.text: Is the characterization in this chapter effective, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: An evaluative judgment with criteria and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Elizabeth now distinguishes between appearance and goodness. Useful evidence: “One has got all the goodness, and the other all the appearance of it” (Chapter XL, paragraph 15): Key line. On characterization: Elizabeth tells Jane of the proposal and the letter but not about Bingley; they decide not to expose Wickham. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
